title: Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution
summary:
Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollutiontoggle caption i Manish Swarup/APNEW DELHI — A thick blanket of smog shrouded India's capital Monday after firecrackers lit up the skies over New Delhi during Diwali celebrations, compounding dangerously high pollution levels and intensifying the seasonal air pollution crisis that grips the city every year.
Sponsor MessageIndia's Supreme Court in October had sought to limit Diwali pollution by restricting conventional firecrackers and allowing only approved "green firecrackers" under specified conditions for three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday.
Isyad, a New Delhi resident who uses one name, said the worsening smog was taking a toll on his health.
Pollution worsens as Diwali fireworks coincide with cooler weather and smoke from crop-residue fires in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana.
The smoke drifts toward New Delhi, adding to pollution from vehicles, industries, construction dust and other local sources.

title: Government's EV targets expected to be reduced this week
summary:
The UK government's electric vehicle (EV) targets are expected to be reduced this week in a move likely to be welcomed by carmakers but opposed by environmental groups.
But the speed of the transition to electric has been hotly debated, including within the cabinet.
Asked about reports the targets would be reduced, Burnham dismissed this as "speculation", adding: "No decision has been made at this point."
The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders welcomed the government's review of the EV targets when it was announced in the summer.
He said the government's targets could not be achieved "without putting at risk any future investment".

title: The superpower battle over energy, and the impact on your bills
summary:
Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.
And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate.
But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK.
Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.
America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them.

title: Daily briefing: The ‘overshoot COP’ kicks off
summary:
The COP31 climate conference begins, with ‘climate overshoot’ a key talking point.
Plus, the surprising benefits of ‘pink noise’ and the role of AI chatbots to support men’s mental health.
(Maximilien Lamy/AFP via Getty)COP climate summit faces overshoot of 1.5 °C A troubling reality hangs over the United Nations climate conference (COP31) opening in Turkey today: overshoot.
Researchers analysed 1,000 conversations between strangers and found that participants felt a stronger sense of connection with their partner when their chats had featured more pink noise.
A separate research team found that pink noise can also help to kickstart the brain’s ‘wash cycle’ during sleep.

title: Turkiye pushes electrification top of climate agenda as COP31 set to open
summary:
Ankara aims to make electricity account for 35 percent of global energy demand by 2035.
Share Turkiye pushes electrification top of climate agenda as COP31 set to open on social mediaThe United Nations climate conference COP31 is set to open on Monday in Antalya, Turkiye, against the backdrop of the US-led war on Iran, which has underscored the world’s attachment to fossil fuels.
Turkiye has said it would centre electrification on the COP31 agenda, launching the non-binding 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, which aims to make electricity account for at least 35 percent of global energy demand by 2035.
Turkiye says the “35 by 35” will speed up the shift to renewable sources of energy while strengthening energy security.
This has set up a debate on whether electrification alone should count as climate progress.

title: The Gloucestershire swan sanctuary fighting climate change
summary:
Most people know rainforests are vital in the fight against climate change, but now scientists say wetlands could be even more important.
Saltmarshes, mangrove swamps and wetlands can absorb carbon "four times faster than trees", according to the charity the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT).
Celebrating 80 years since WWT's first wetland bird reserve was founded at Slimbridge, in Gloucestershire, the charity's leaders have called for one million hectares of wetlands to be restored across the world.
Sarah Fowler, CEO of WWT, said: "They are mood-boosting, flood-buffering, water-purifying, incredible habitats.
But we have lost 85% of the world's wetlands."

summary:
NewsFeed COP31 opens amid energy crisis as activists demand climate actionCOP31 has opened in Turkiye amid war-driven energy disruptions and a renewed reliance on fossil fuels.
While delegates discuss electrification and climate action, activists outside the summit are demanding an end to greenwashing and a shift away from industrial agriculture.

title: Smog blankets New Delhi as Diwali firecrackers worsen air quality
summary:
Air quality in Indian capital reaches severe levels, posing heightened health risks for more than 30 million residents.
Share Smog blankets New Delhi as Diwali firecrackers worsen air quality on social mediaHeavy smog has blanketed New Delhi after firecrackers lit up the Indian capital during Diwali celebrations, worsening the seasonal pollution crisis.
Last month, India’s Supreme Court put in place restrictions to limit Diwali pollution, allowing only approved “green firecrackers” under specified conditions for three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday.
Seasonal pollutionOn Wednesday, days before Diwali, toxic air pollution in New Delhi surged to more than 30 times the WHO’s recommended daily limit, data from air monitors showed.
AdvertisementVehicles account for 23 percent of New Delhi’s winter pollution, while biomass burning, including farm stubble fires, contributes 20 percent, according to India’s Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.

title: North Pennines National Landscape prepares for climate change
summary:
Climate change readiness and helping people access the countryside are among priorities in a five-year plan for a national landscape.
The North Pennines National Landscape Management Plan 2026-31 has been adopted by the Cumberland, Westmorland and Furness, County Durham and Northumberland councils.
Chris Woodley-Stewart, director of the North Pennines National Landscape (NPNL), said: "In many ways, its the most ambitious plan that we've ever had, but also the most realistic."
National landscapes were formerly known as areas of outstanding natural beauty, and the North Pennines features heather moors, dales, woods and one of England's highest waterfalls High Force.
One of the priorities in its management plan announced last month was adapting to "warmer, wetter winters and hotter, drier summers".

title: Global fossil fuel emissions set to fall in 2026, but total CO2 keeps rising
summary:
The report estimates that fossil fuel emissions will total 38.2 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) in 2026.
Even so, researchers caution that the transition is not happening quickly enough to guarantee a lasting reduction in fossil fuel emissions.
Fossil Fuel Emissions Fall, but Total CO 2 Keeps RisingDespite the projected decline in fossil fuel emissions, the overall picture is more troubling.
Carbon Emissions in China, the US, India, and EuropeThe 2026 Global Carbon Budget reveals significant differences in how emissions are changing across major economies.
It provides a transparent assessment of global carbon emissions using established scientific methods and undergoes peer review.

title: Scientists discover stunning new Amazon fish that may already be endangered
summary:
The new species, named Laimosemion laranja, belongs to a group of small freshwater fish known as killifish.
Although the fish looked different from known species, its appearance alone was not enough to establish that it was new to science.
Why Scientists Named the New Fish LaranjaThe name Laimosemion laranja reflects both the fish's remarkable appearance and the place where it was discovered.
"Laimosemion laranja is particularly interesting because it expands our knowledge of the diversity and evolution of this group in the region."
Newly Discovered Amazon Fish May Already Be EndangeredDespite the excitement surrounding the discovery, the future of Laimosemion laranja is uncertain.

title: El Niño pushes world towards record heat as COP31 opens
summary:
The world is on course for its hottest year on record as the planet is hit with warming from climate change and El Niño, scientists have told BBC News.
The warning comes as world leaders and negotiators gather in Turkey on Monday for the opening of COP31, the latest UN climate summit.
"We have had a run of record warm years," said Dr Robert Rohde, of Berkeley Earth.
On Friday, the EU's Copernicus climate service, external confirmed that October was the hottest on record.
It said that 2027 will provide no let-up, as an unusually powerful El Niño will continue into next year, pushing temperatures higher.

title: Who’s Winning (and Who’s Losing) the Ocean? — Marie-May Jeremie
summary:
When frontier AI labs go public, ordinary people’s investments and pensions become tied to their valuations and stock prices.
While excessive regulation could undermine a firm’s growth, catastrophic accidents caused by inadequate safety measures could do the same—and wipe out shareholder value.
points out that ordinary investors will have direct financial incentives to demand robust safety measures.
